title: Food, sacrifice, austerity, gift — three kinds each (17.7–17.22)
hook: the Gita sorts your lunch, your worship, your discipline and your giving into three kinds

segments.voice: Yesterday, shraddha: a person is made of faith, and faith follows nature. Today, the three threads come to the kitchen table.

Open the fridge at midnight. There's the leftover takeout from three days ago. There are the extra-spicy chips that'll burn all the way down. And there's a bowl of warm rice and dal someone made with care. A hand hovers. A holy book might seem to have nothing to say here. The Gita does. Having said that faith comes in three kinds, chapter seventeen applies the three threads to four ordinary things: what you eat, how you worship, how you discipline yourself, and how you give.
screen: `THE FRIDGE AT MIDNIGHT.` → `LEFTOVERS, CHIPS, OR WARM DAL?` → `THE GITA HAS AN OPINION.`

segments.voice: Food first. Verse eight: sattvic food lengthens life and brings purity, strength, health, happiness and cheer. It's tasty, smooth, nourishing and pleasant. Verse nine: rajasic food is bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry and burning. It brings pain, grief and sickness. Verse ten: tamasic food is stale, flavorless, spoiled, leftover, impure. Some commentators read that 'very' as reaching across the whole list, so the trouble is excess, not flavor. Then sacrifice, the offering. Sattvic: done because it ought to be done, not for a reward. Rajasic: done for the reward, or for show. Tamasic: done carelessly, without faith, without the proper words, without sharing food with others. Then austerity, tapas, discipline, in three places. Of the body: honoring teachers, cleanliness, straightness, doing no harm. Of speech, verse fifteen: words that don't upset people, that are true, kind and helpful. Of the mind: calm, gentleness, silence, self-control. Done with faith and no wish for reward, it's sattvic. Done for honor and praise, rajasic. Done to torture yourself or harm someone else, tamasic. And last, the gift. Verse twenty: a gift given simply because it should be given, to someone who can't pay you back, at the right time and place, to the right person, is sattvic. Given to get something back, or grudgingly: rajasic. Given with contempt, at the wrong time, to the wrong person: tamasic. So the week closes: tejas, the light in the sun, the one beyond, the divine and the demonic, the scripture, faith, and now food.
screen: `FOOD: NOURISHING, TOO MUCH, STALE.` · `SACRIFICE: DUTY, SHOW, CARELESS.` · `AUSTERITY OF BODY, SPEECH, MIND.` · `THE GIFT THAT WANTS NOTHING BACK.` · then, large: `FOOD.`

segments.voice: Think of your last meal: did it leave you light and clear, buzzing or burning, heavy and dull? No judgment, just notice. Then think of the last thing you gave someone, time, money, a favor, whether you hoped for something back, and hold in mind one small gift you could give to someone who can't repay you.
Food. Gita seventeen: food, sacrifice, austerity and gift each come in three kinds, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, and the kind shapes the one who eats, offers or gives.
Your line: which kind. Plate, offering, discipline or gift, each comes in three. Day two hundred seventeen, done.

howItsDone: Some Hindus think about food in terms of the three gunas, preferring fresh, simple, sattvic food, especially before worship; Gita 17.20's gift given without hope of return is cited in teaching on dana, charity.

match.prompt: three kinds each — tap the pairs.
pairs: to one who can't pay you back

myth: in Gita 17, stale and spoiled food is called tamasic
verse 10: stale, flavorless, spoiled, leftover, impure.
Gita 17.15 describes austerity of speech: true, kind and helpful words
words that don't upset, that are true, pleasant and beneficial.
a gift given in hope of a return is still sattvic

fork.setup: you want to give a gift the Gita would call sattvic. who do you give it to?
options: someone who'll do you a favor later.
someone who can't pay you back, at the right time and place.
whoever will praise you for it.
fork.reveal: verse 20: a gift given because it should be given, to one who can't repay, at the right place and time.

original.note: Sanskrit: sattvika, of the nature of sattva: clear, nourishing, balanced. the same pattern gives rajasika and tamasika.

trapdoor: what you thought: this chapter is a diet plan.
what it means: food, worship, discipline and giving each come in three kinds, and each shapes the person.

what a scholar hears: 17.8–17.10 on food, 17.11–17.13 on yajna, 17.14–17.19 on tapas of body, speech and mind, 17.20–17.22 on dana; 17.20 specifies giving to one who cannot return the favor (anupakarine).
guess: nourishment that comes in three kinds and shapes the eater
an offering left for the gods that's never to be eaten
a fast kept on holy days to purify the body
